title: Will we have enough attention for so many games? And what about the future of MMOs and online games in general?
author: ImpressionanteFato
selftext:
I've been seeing a lot of game projects being made with the help of AI, and don't get me wrong, I think that's incredible. I'm not 100% pro AI, I'm 1,000% pro AI. But one thing that worries me a little is whether we'll actually have enough human players and enough attention to go around for all these games being released, plus all the ones that haven't come out yet but will over the next few days, months, and years.

Especially online games like MMORPGs, which need players to keep their ecosystems alive. Some need more players than others, obviously, but most of them still need a minimum number of active players for the whole ecosystem to work the way it's supposed to.

Or do you think that for projects like MMOs, developers might eventually start using AI players mixed in with human players?

And when I say AI here, I mean LLMs, not the traditional AI we've had in games for decades.

I recently saw the release of the Liquid LFM3 model, which is ridiculously small and can fit in around 2GB of RAM. It doesn't even necessarily need VRAM to run locally.

That got me thinking. With hardware constantly improving, LLMs constantly getting optimized, and small models becoming more and more capable, could we reach a point in 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 years or more where online games have massive numbers of AI players?

AI players that, just from chatting and interacting with them, would be basically impossible to distinguish from a real human player?

And maybe at an almost negligible cost for companies to implement?

When it comes to AI, I'm extremely optimistic. It's one of the few things in the universe where I'm probably annoyingly optimistic lol.

Even if 1,000 people told me something like this would take 10 or 30 years, if I had to bet, I'd say within a year at most we'll already start seeing something along these lines becoming practical and cheap for companies to use.

And in this case, I think "practical" and "cheap" kind of need to exist together for it to actually happen on a large scale, if that makes any sense lol.

I'd really like to hear what you guys think about this.

**PS:** I'm not trying to discourage anyone. If you're making an online game, no matter what genre it is, keep going.

These are just crazy theories and assumptions.

As the years go by, we'll also have more humans alive, more people growing up, becoming adults, getting into games, and so on. So it's VERY possible that we'll never even get close to a point where massive numbers of AI players are actually necessary.

But if something like this were going to be implemented on a large scale, my guess for the timeline would still be what I mentioned above.

That doesn't mean I think there will actually be a real need for it to happen.

comments.body: Most games are slop though. The actual good games being released will always have players

replies.author: EinArchitekt
replies.body: I think a good game alone is not enough. There are a lot of examples where great games, especially multiplayer, dies out. Most recent examples I remember are Supervive and Hyperscape.

replies.author: cheyumaama
replies.body: What's so special about supervive? Yeah it looks good, but games like that exist. Does it have a story mode at least that makes it playable as a single player? No. And they had players. It's not like they didn't have players. They just were going for a League of Legends/Fortnite model and it didn't work out. Most of our games aren't going for that kinda model anyway. Hyper scape looks good too but again, these are free to play multiplayer games that make money by selling skins or whatever. Battle royale multiplayers that require a constant player base to survive isn't gonna be what most of us are making

i also found this odd. its like the least accessible, requires way more resources and time and dedication, and way more players. 

Hard enough getting new players to commit time to any new game, let alone a MMO lol 

But on the other hand, 99.9% of these games will "fail" (from a commercial standpoint) anyway, and making some of these games in just as much (or more) fun than playing a game, so who am I to judge

replies.author: niloony
replies.body: Some people are committed to failing regardless of the additional assistance they're given. User acquisition is the hardest thing about an MMO, a singleplayer indie game can chug along with an active community at like 20 CCU, an MMO needs hundreds at least for playtesting. Plus the active community IS the gameplay.

comments.author: Hot_Professional8287
comments.body:
\>But one thing that worries me a little is whether we'll actually have enough human players

I wouldn't worry. I think the market's quality expectations will become much higher.

The quantity you're seeing today is AI-mimicry of pre-AI product quality, attempting to push into the market. When indies learn to pour Eric Barone tier levels of focus and energy into quality AI-assisted game development, it will move the market upwards. The quantity you see today will become the background noise of people just messing around and learning the craft. I think it'll be like the pre-LLM market again. Still highly competitive, but mind-reeling levels of quality for the titles near the top.

comments.author: Lumpy_Conference6640
comments.body:
SO! I have strong feelings about this one. First, the level of impact versus return. Let's throw out the sloppers. Let's talk about people really doing the work. 

1. Business Use Case: Barrier to entry is much lower.. RoI is potentially huge. This as been the BIGGEST risk factor in the industry thus far. 

2. MMORPG. I'm rebuilding some legacy MMO's with AI Players.. "giving that feel" of a populated universe without needing to make critical player counts. 

3. Remasters... there's a literal gold mine of historic game formats that can be refactored toward new vibes, with proven gaming formats. It's mind-blowing; I'm remastering one of my childhood favorites right now, and it's amazing!

4. Prompt Libraries... at this point, $120 can buy a lot of tokens if used right, and you should be able to complete tailored individual gaming experiences on purchase. That's the real market for high-level gaming.

replies.body:

comments.author: re-skob
comments.body: games will get a lot more niche and personalized with smaller communities around them. Now there could be games that only 10k - 20k players play and those will be considered pretty successful and if you could make a few a year sold at 1.99 or 2.99 or something then it'll be a decent living, some games will still be huge tentpole games that still take a year or a couple to make and those will be played by millions. Look at YouTube, there is more content coming out on YouTube that can be viewed in a lifetime but there are still lots of people getting millions of views. In the same vein, games will also get a lot shorter. You don't need to make a game last 1000 hours, you could make serialized games, maybe 30 minutes of content, maybe an hour and release a new episode every week.

comments.author: CycleMother2006
comments.body:
Online games are fine. Mid/large scoped games are fine. No scope indie games are going to drown amongst a deluge of filth because there's no barrier for AI in creating them.

MMOs are an exception to the mid/large scoped games being fine comment. Other games are much cheaper to make now with AI assistance. But MMOs have costs far beyond their development, and those costs aren't changing. They also demand high player counts to maintain a feeling of the world being alive and usually to drive their systems.

I  personally think its foolish to go into the MMO genre unless you're Riot or some equally large company that has reach both in the gaming world AND can potentially pull in a new wave of casual gamers that are interested in the franchise as a whole.



Don't get too attached to the pace of AI development we've had the last few years. It's already slowed. Hardware constraints are real and the GPUs in the early datacenters from a couple years ago are hitting the peak of their die off. They're going to need replacements, and there's already a big shortage. The compute required for training new models is huge, and it's not feasible for them to continue doing that, WHILE offering compute to subs, WHILE also being unable to get chips for more powerful AI. Expect the focus of AI development to shift towards efficiency (JEV, for instance, being a key example) rather than trying to keep pushing up the capabilities. That's not even including fears of AI superintelligence and all that.

  
So I personally think things are going to ease up. The barrier of entry has lifted, but there is still work involved in real projects. "Work" is anathema to a lot of the people pushing get-rich-quick slop, and when they oversaturate themselves and can't make money they'll just move to greener pastures instead of trying to develop something real.  We saw something similar when Unity first became a real engine and with its  effectively free model you had a bunch of random developers hopping in, throwing together some shitty level, throwing a bunch of CC0 assets in, and trying to sell it as early access in the marketplace. There are still games up there that were part of that asset flip era which have long since been abandonware. This feels quite similar.
